sections.heading: Thanking you for ruling over everything and stooping down to me
sections.text: Father, you rule over everything I can see and everything I cannot see. I come to you grateful and amazed that you would come near to someone like me. Your grace still surprises me. You have not let me forget what you did when you first opened my eyes and comforted my heart.
theological_themes: God reigns over both the visible and invisible creation.
Grace is not earned; God stoops down in mercy to save and comfort the undeserving.
Remembering conversion can become fresh fuel for worship and gratitude.

scripture_references.connection: Paul presents Christ as Lord over all created things, visible and invisible, holding everything together. This supports the prayer’s opening confidence that God’s rule extends over all reality.
This passage grounds salvation in God’s rich mercy and love toward people who were spiritually dead. It fits the prayer’s wonder that God would show grace to the helpless and undeserving.

sections.heading: Remembering how you rescued me when I had no way out
sections.text: I remember when you brought me through a way I never would have expected. It was like standing at the edge of the sea with danger behind me and no strength in myself, and then you made a path. I had nearly given up hope, but you delivered me from fear and brought me into the first real comfort I had ever known in you. Remembering it still fills me with joy.
theological_themes: Conversion is God’s rescue, not self-improvement or self-deliverance.
God often saves in ways his people could not have planned or imagined.
Remembering past deliverance strengthens present joy and faith.

scripture_references.connection: Israel’s passage through the Red Sea is the concrete image behind this section: God made a way of deliverance when his people were trapped and afraid. The prayer uses that event as a picture of personal rescue by grace.
Paul describes salvation as being delivered from the domain of darkness and brought into Christ’s kingdom. That gives a New Testament frame for speaking of conversion as rescue from bondage and fear.

sections.heading: Admitting how much I needed you then, and still need you now
sections.text: When I look back, my heart softens. I was poor, helpless, and empty of wisdom. I did not know how to guide myself, and I had no power to save myself. Yet that helplessness became a mercy, because it forced me to lean on you. And when I had nothing in myself, I found that your comfort was not small or thin, but wide and generous.
theological_themes: Human helplessness exposes the need for God’s saving and sustaining grace.
Weakness can become a mercy when it drives a person to depend on God.
God’s comfort is abundant for those who have no resources in themselves.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes being so burdened that he despaired of life, so that he would rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead. This closely matches the prayer’s memory of helplessness becoming the place where dependence on God was learned.
Christ tells Paul that his grace is sufficient and his power is made perfect in weakness. This supports the prayer’s claim that the believer’s lack of strength is met by God’s abundant help.

sections.heading: Finding everything I need in you
sections.text: Lord Jesus, you are my true treasure. All fullness is in you. You are my life, my hope, my joy, my peace, my glory, and my final home. Keep teaching my heart to stop treating you as one help among many, and to know you as my whole portion.
theological_themes: Christ is not merely a giver of gifts; he himself is the believer’s treasure and portion.
All saving fullness is found in Christ.
The Christian life is centered on finding life, hope, peace, and joy in him.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell in Christ, through whom God reconciles all things. This grounds the prayer’s language about Christ as the treasury of all fullness.

Paul counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him. That supports the prayer’s desire to have Christ as the believer’s supreme treasure rather than merely one benefit among others.

sections.heading: Asking to become more like Christ and ready for heaven
sections.text: Make me more like you day by day. Put the meekness and quiet strength of the Lamb into my soul. Let me taste, even now, something of the happiness of heaven, where I will be free from sin and weakness, where your image in me will finally be made whole, and where I will be ready for every joy and every work you have for your people.
theological_themes: Sanctification is daily conformity to Christ.
Christ’s meekness is not weakness but holy gentleness and calm strength.
The hope of heaven includes complete restoration into Christ’s likeness and freedom from remaining sin.

scripture_references.connection: Believers are being transformed into the Lord’s image from one degree of glory to another. This directly supports the prayer’s request for daily conformity to Christ.

John teaches that when Christ appears, believers will be like him because they will see him as he is, and this hope purifies them now. That connects future perfection with present holiness, just as the prayer does.
The final vision of God’s servants includes worship, service, seeing God’s face, and reigning with him. This supports the prayer’s language about being fitted for the joys and employments of heaven.

sections.heading: Facing death with hope and wanting my life to praise you
sections.text: Because of you, I do not need to stare at death as though it owns me. When my time comes, I want to leave this world as one drawn home by you, not dragged away in terror. Until then, let my life burn steadily for you. And when that last great change comes, let me wake in your likeness. Leave behind, if you are pleased to do it, a life that helps others honor you—not because I was great, but because you were merciful to me. Let those who remember me have reason to praise you.
theological_themes: Death is real and fearful in itself, but Christ gives believers hope beyond it.
The Christian’s desire is to spend life in devotion to God until the end.
A faithful life can continue to bear witness to God’s grace after death.
The ultimate hope is to awake in God’s likeness and rejoice in his presence.

scripture_references.connection: Paul can face death with hope because departing means being with Christ, while continued life means fruitful labor. This supports both the prayer’s lack of terror before death and its desire to keep living usefully for God until then.
The psalmist looks forward to beholding God’s face and being satisfied with his likeness when he awakes. This closely supports the prayer’s hope of waking in God’s likeness after death.

Abel’s faith still speaks after his death, showing that a life lived before God can continue to bear witness. This supports the prayer’s request that what remains after death would lead others to praise God.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s phrase about the believer’s memory being blessed on earth could be misunderstood as a desire for personal reputation or posthumous honor. I rendered it as a desire that others would praise God for his mercy shown in the person’s life.

The original’s confidence about not fearing death is strong. I preserved that confidence while avoiding the implication that a Christian will necessarily experience the dying process without emotional struggle or physical pain.
significant_interpretive_choices: The Red Sea language was treated as a metaphor for conversion and spiritual deliverance, not as a claim that the author literally experienced an Exodus-like event.
The phrase 'drawn, not driven, out of the world' was interpreted as hopeful, willing departure into God’s presence by grace, rather than being forced away by terror.
The request to be fitted for heaven’s 'enjoyments and employments' was rendered as being ready for both the joys and the service God gives his people in the renewed creation.
